method: Read all 18 assigned target/context sources in full from preserved HTML, including XML date attributes and people, exclusions, footnotes, apparatus, scholarly siblings, bibliographies and available inline figures. Compared each Darwin target backward against distinctive incoming content and kept public, institutional, logistical, receipt and reading stages separate. No relationship was inferred from topic overlap or packet adjacency.

outgoing_reviews.title: To Frederick Watkins 18 August 1832
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Watkins for a long account of home and friends, while recounting Cape Verde, Brazil, Buenos Aires unrest and the planned Patagonia survey. It is a personal request for news, with no surviving Watkins response in this scope.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To F. W. Hope 1 November 1833
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin apologizes for delayed contact, reports tropical and southern collecting, asks Hope for scientific-entomological gossip and gives the Beagle address. His insect account and request are directed to Hope.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To Edward Lumb 30 March 1834
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Lumb to trace the forwarding time and ship of Keen’s Megatherium bones, adds geological travel news and asks for political and local gossip. The cargo-routing question is concrete and logistical.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To Charles Whitley 23 July 1834
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin renews contact with Whitley, jokes about politics and the voyage, describes South American scenery and Fuegian encounters, and asks for Cambridge and personal news. No particular scientific answer is required.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To H. S. Fox 15 August 1835
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin sends H. S. Fox specimens and asks about elevated marine shells and geology in Brazil, alongside a detailed account of Cordilleran geology and his route home. The source is a scientific request, but no matching Fox answer is in the assigned scope.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To Alexander Burns Usborne [c. 1–5 September 1835]
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin gives Usborne field criteria for distinguishing raised marine shell beds from transported shells, requests labelled rocks and careful elevations, and specifies observations useful to the geological survey. This is an instruction letter with no incoming Usborne text here.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: 1 inline figure element(s) in preserved body HTML; no uninspected figure was used.

outgoing_reviews.title: To Phillip Parker King [21 January 1836]
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin tells King of his hot overland journey, possible delay, geology and a successful platypus hunt, planning to visit him at Dunheved. It is a visit notice and travel update rather than a response to a preserved King prompt.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To South African Christian Recorder 28 June 1836
outgoing_reviews.summary: This public statement, signed jointly by FitzRoy and Darwin, supports Pacific missionaries after balancing reported and observed evidence. It has institutional/public voice and no private incoming prompt.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To Charles Whitley 24 October [1836]
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin acknowledges Whitley’s letter and marriage, discusses an undelivered letter to Herbert, his return and specimen workload, and asks for more detail and Herbert’s address. The earlier Whitley exchange needed for the marriage news is not the 1834 target alone.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To The Master & Fellows, Caius College [19 December 1836 – 6 March 1837]
outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin’s short institutional note declines a Caius dinner because of a prior engagement. It contains no scientific or correspondence prompt.
outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

outgoing_reviews.title: To Anthony Carlisle [19 December 1836]
outgoing_reviews.summary: The preserved text is a record of Darwin’s 19 December offer of Beagle fossil bones, with conditions about casts for public bodies; its presentation in a college record must be kept distinct from a conventional private ALS.

authority.label: Charles Darwin (letter recorded in institutional minute)

outgoing_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

incoming_reviews.title: From Henry Stephen Fox 31 October 1833
incoming_reviews.summary: Fox urges Darwin to visit Flores, describes its greenstone and sends Porto Alegre specimens with geological observations, asking Darwin for rocks from Magellan and Chile. The source is a direct scientific exchange, but no subsequent assigned Darwin response is identified.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

incoming_reviews.title: From F. W. Hope 15 January 1834
incoming_reviews.summary: Hope explicitly acknowledges Darwin’s 1 November letter, discusses insect geography and volcanic conditions, requests broad collecting of larvae, Hymenoptera and Diptera, and reports the Entomological Society and scientific news. It answers the entomological content of 227 while adding independent requests.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

incoming_reviews.title: From Edward Lumb 13 November 1833
incoming_reviews.summary: Lumb acknowledges Darwin’s 5 November letter, explains why prohibited shot and powder could not be sent, reports the chart and goods arrangements, and gives incomplete information about fish off Cape Corrientes. It is a logistical response to an unassigned Darwin letter, not to 241’s later Megatherium request.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

incoming_reviews.title: From Edward Lumb 8 May 1834
incoming_reviews.summary: Lumb says he received Darwin’s 30 March letter and responds to its Falklands political report and the bones: he names the Basenthwaite shipment to Henslow, bill of lading, duplicate forwarding plan and Hooker’s expected collection. Later political and family news is separate from the cargo answer.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

incoming_reviews.title: From H. S. Fox 25 July 1834
incoming_reviews.summary: Fox thanks Darwin for his 5 April East Falkland letter and specimens, promises a future answer to geological queries about Rio Grande and southern Brazil, and supplies contextual scientific contacts. This is a response to an unassigned Darwin letter, not to 284’s later request.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

incoming_reviews.title: From Charles Whitley 5 February 1835
incoming_reviews.summary: Whitley answers a prior Darwin letter, describing his Durham professorship, friends, church reform and personal news, and complains that Darwin has not written. The extensive social content does not identify 250’s 1834 prompt; an intervening Whitley letter is missing from this scope.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

incoming_reviews.title: From Anthony Carlisle 23 December 1836
incoming_reviews.summary: Carlisle reports that he submitted Darwin’s 19 December letter to the Board of Curators, which approved its terms and recommended acceptance to the College Council. This is an institutional acknowledgment of 330’s recorded offer, not evidence that every college stage is complete.
incoming_reviews.figure_note: No inline figure was present in the preserved HTML.

proposed_links.scope: Hope’s P2 and P3 answer the entomological report and collecting concerns in Darwin’s 1 November letter; this is a scoped exchange and does not make Hope’s later Society news an answer to every paragraph.

evidence.quote: Your letter of Nov 1st. 1833, has just come to hand
If, as I believe you told me, Europæan cabinets contain few of the minuter Beetles from tropical countries

proposed_links.scope: Lumb’s P2-P3 directly acknowledge the 30 March letter and answer its Megatherium-bone forwarding question. Political and family material is outside the supported cargo scope.

evidence.quote: I duly recd. your favour of the 30 March from the Falklands
By the brig “Basenthwaite” Mitchinson Martin for Liverpool I forwarded the Bones and Specimens recd. from Mr. Keen carefully packed
I am very anxious that the Megatherium head, which Mr Keen procured for me

proposed_links.scope: Carlisle’s institutional reply confirms submission and Curators’ approval of Darwin’s 19 December fossil offer. It supports the acceptance stage only; Council decision and physical transfer remain prospective.

evidence.quote: I have had the satisfaction to submit your Letter of the 19th. to the Board of Curators who expressed their intire approval of the terms and conditions annexed to your highly liberal offer
a Series of fossil Bones collected during the voyage of H:M: Surveying Vessel Beagle possesses a peculiar Interest

findings: DCP-LETT-227 → DCP-LETT-235 and DCP-LETT-241 → DCP-LETT-245 are direct scoped replies explicitly naming the incoming dates.
DCP-LETT-330 → DCP-LETT-334 is an institutional acceptance-stage exchange; the target body is a recorded offer and Carlisle’s response does not establish final Council acceptance or transfer.

DCP-LETT-226, DCP-LETT-252 and DCP-LETT-267 refer to Darwin letters outside this assigned target set; they were retained as context and not reassigned to later targets. DCP-LETT-284’s geological request likewise lacks a matching incoming answer here.

DCP-LETT-250 and DCP-LETT-314 are both Darwin-to-Whitley letters, so they cannot be treated as an inbound-to-Darwin exchange; 314 acknowledges an intervening Whitley letter not preserved in this scope.
DCP-LETT-303 is jointly signed public speech; DCP-LETT-326 is an institutional dinner note; neither supplies a private prompt.
DCP-LETT-285 is a detailed field instruction to Usborne, and DCP-LETT-293 is a travel notice to King; no surviving incoming text supports a reply edge.
limitations: No unassigned letters were promoted into this report. Exact receipt dates remain those supported by body or XML; bounded dates for 285 and 326 are preserved. Figure checks found no body figure for most sources; any figure elements present were inspected only as source availability, not treated as textual evidence.
